source.title: Inverse scaling can become U-shaped
source.authors: Jason Wei; Najoung Kim; Yi Tay; Quoc V. Le

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream performance across model sizes using task accuracy or loss, rather than testing held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates PaLM on inverse-scaling benchmark tasks and reports task-level results by model size and prompt condition. These are downstream-task outcomes, not held-out pretraining loss, compute-optimal allocation, or architecture comparisons. Cited scaling-law results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates PaLM 1B–540B on eleven downstream tasks (Table 2). These results bear directly on whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale (V6). Four tasks scale inversely, six are U-shaped and one improves under default prompting, so the version needs restating. The tasks were chosen because they scaled inversely in other model families, so they are adversarially selected rather than representative. No pretraining loss is measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors say six of eleven Inverse Scaling Prize tasks become U-shaped at 540B, four stay inverse and one scales positively. They conclude inverse-scaling curves need not extrapolate to larger models, which they attribute speculatively to distractor tasks. They add that 1-shot demonstrations turn all inverse tasks U-shaped or flat, CoT turns several positive, and scaling combined with prompting can mitigate inverse scaling.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates downstream benchmark tasks across PaLM sizes and prompt conditions; it does not fit pretraining-loss power laws or compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Scaling patterns vary by task and prompting condition; 1-shot demonstrations change the reported patterns on tasks that remained inverse scaling under default prompting.
record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The results concern selected downstream tasks rather than pretraining loss. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The authors note that some task performance remains near chance or poor, and describe their distractor-task explanation as speculative.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix A, Table 2 also reports official 1-shot results for the other seven tasks, controlled 1-shot results, and 1-shot CoT results for ten tasks. These are omitted to stay within the 60-row limit after retaining all default-prompt task-by-size results and official 1-shot results for the four tasks that changed from inverse scaling. Section 3 and Appendix A, Table 2 report the omitted prompting conditions.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss is measured.
No pretraining-loss power-law fits are made or extrapolated.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is not studied.
No other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream performance against pretraining loss; downstream predictability on tasks not selected for inverse scaling.
No fitting choices or exponents are examined.

missing.what: 1-shot CoT results. Under CoT, Negation QA, Into the unknown, Pattern matching suppression, Redefine and Hindsight Neglect become positive; Modus tollens is flat and saturated; Memo trap, Resisting correction and Pattern matching end non-monotonic. This bears on V6 prompt dependence.
Official 1-shot results for the seven tasks other than the four default-inverse ones (mostly U-shaped; Repetitive algebra positive), and controlled 1-shot results for all tasks.
Ten-task average accuracy against compute and parameters, which is U-shaped for PaLM.

record.verdict_notes: The tasks were selected because they scaled inversely in other model families, so the V6 challenge holds for adversarially chosen tasks, not tasks in general. PaLM 1B was trained on only 40B tokens, versus 780B for the larger models. Its high scores on some tasks may therefore reflect near-chance behaviour, and token count is confounded with size. Per-size rows were assigned the state of their task's curve, since a single size cannot show a trend. Results for Gopher, Chinchilla and Anthropic models in Figure 2 are cited from McKenzie et al. and should not be rows. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation of pretraining-loss power-law fits from small to large runs.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study tests downstream task performance against model size on selected inverse-scaling tasks, but not downstream performance against pretraining loss or general predictability across tasks.
Does not test pretraining-loss fit exponents, compute-optimal allocation, or their dependence on setup and fitting choices.
